messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-four when his fiancée—a woman he had known since college, whom he had trusted completely—broke three of his ribs and fractured his left orbital bone during an argument in their shared apartment. He had come home late from a shift, and she had been drinking. He remembered the smell of whiskey on her breath as she confronted him about his phone, remembered her voice rising, then the first blow coming from an angle he did not anticipate. What struck him most, in the months afterward, was not the physical pain but the realization that he had not seen it coming. He was a detective. He read people for a living. He had missed everything.

Marcus was now twenty-six and had been married to someone new for eighteen months—a careful, gentle marriage built on what he believed was mutual understanding. Yet the person he had become bore little resemblance to the man his wife had married. He moved through their home like a ghost, present in body but absent in every way that mattered. When she reached for his hand during a movie, he would stiffen and pull away, offering some excuse about his shoulder being sore. When she tried to massage his neck, he felt his throat tighten with something close to panic. Any touch, no matter how tender its intention, registered as a threat his body could not ignore.

The nausea came without warning. A colleague would mention grabbing drinks after work, and the smell of beer on someone's clothes would hit him as he passed their desk, and suddenly his stomach would turn. He would excuse himself to the bathroom, gripping the sink, waiting for the sensation to pass. He had come to avoid the break room entirely, had stopped attending departmental happy hours years ago. His captain had stopped asking.

But worse than the nausea were the moments when he would see something that made his mind travel backward. A suspect with a black eye. A domestic violence victim with bruises blooming across her shoulders. These images would lodge in his consciousness and pull up something older—not just a memory, but a full sensory reconstruction. He would hear the sound of her voice, sharp and slurred, the specific timbre of rage. The memory was not vague or distant; it was vivid enough that he could feel the impact again, could taste blood in his mouth. These intrusions came without permission, forcing themselves into his mind while he was trying to write a report or interview a witness. He had learned to excuse himself, to find a bathroom or an empty office, to wait until the episode passed.

What had calcified over time was something deeper than fear. Marcus had come to believe that people were fundamentally unknowable, that the version of someone you saw was always a performance, a carefully constructed lie. His wife loved him, he supposed, but he did not trust what love meant anymore. He had loved his fiancée. He had been completely wrong. This certainty—that he had been fundamentally foolish, that his judgment was broken, that he could never truly know another person—had become the lens through which he viewed all relationships. He felt like an outsider in his own marriage, a man who had learned a terrible truth that others had not yet discovered.

He had stopped trying to relax. The moment he felt his body begin to soften, some part of him would panic. Relaxation felt like vulnerability, like lowering his guard, and lowering his guard was how he had gotten hurt. Instead, he numbed himself methodically—not with alcohol, which he could no longer bear the smell of, but with work, with distance, with the careful construction of emotional walls. His wife had stopped trying to reach him. She had stopped asking what was wrong.

Marcus came to therapy because his wife had given him an ultimatum, delivered quietly and without anger: either he got help, or she would leave. He sat in the first session with his hands clenched, his jaw tight, afraid that talking about what happened would somehow make it more real, more present. What he feared most was that nothing would change, that he would remain permanently fractured, unable to trust, unable to let anyone close. What he hoped for, though he could barely articulate it, was to feel safe in his own skin again, and to understand how that was even possible.
